extracted.intended_audience: novelists; serious students of fiction; creative writers studying narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and managing narrative methods in the novel (pictorial narration vs dramatic enactment), use of first person, and how to dramatize narrator and inner life. Focuses on when to show vs tell and how to combine methods to strengthen a novel's effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice between pictorial narration and dramatic enactment
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of picture-making enables the novelist to cover his great spaces of life and quantities of experience, while drama is limited but offers intensity of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pictorial/narrative method when you need breadth, panoramic coverage, memory or consciousness to present many facts at once; use dramatic enactment when you need immediacy and intensity. Be aware of the trade-off: pictorial gives scope but risks loss of intensity; drama gives intensity but is limited in scope. Examples: Fielding, Balzac, George Eliot lean to picture; Tolstoy and Dostoevsky lean to scenic/dramatic methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve drama for important occasions
rubrics_metrics.description: Drama is the novelist’s highest light... to use it prodigally where it is not needed is to lessen its force where it is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hoard dramatic scenes rather than using them constantly; deploy enactment for climaxes or moments that need emphasis (example cited: Bovary). Overuse reduces dramatic force; economy increases impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid a conspicuous omniscient author
rubrics_metrics.description: In its plain form [pictorial method] it drags in the omniscient author and may make him exceedingly conspicuous, producing a kind of thinness in the general impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimize intrusive authorial commentary unless the author's personality is a deliberate and effective feature of the book. If the omniscient voice is too visible it undermines the authority and objectivity of the picture; only charm/genius can compensate consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize the narrator (make the recorder an active presence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author might treat his view as though it were in its turn a piece of action... it would be like a play within a play; the outer framework — consisting of the reflective mind — would be immediately in front of the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of letting a detached narrator report, bring the narrator's act of remembering or judging into the scene as action. Making the narrator a dramatized, measurable presence authenticates and enhances the picture and adds an independent interest (Thackeray’s later work and Esmond are cited as examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use first person to give precision, individuality, and bounded vision
rubrics_metrics.description: The characterized 'I' is substituted for the loose and general 'I' of the author; precision, individuality is given to the picture by this pair of eyes, known and named.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First person fixes a field of vision and supplies personal colour and tone; it makes the vantage point measurable and often more convincing for pictorial works where a named, limited perspective is desirable (examples: Esmond, David Copperfield).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use first-person/autobiographical mode to unify rambling or episodic material
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of the first person composes of its own accord; the hero gives the story an indefeasible unity by the mere act of telling it... Autobiography's charm is its fidelity to the winding course of the writer's thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a novel is a long glance or chronicle of episodes, first person can unify disparate incidents and make a rambling, fragmentary tale feel coherent. Beware: this advantage can disguise weaknesses of form and can legitimize formlessness if misused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overtax first-person when the narrator must also be the central subject
rubrics_metrics.description: When the man in the book is expected to make a picture of himself, a searching and elaborate portrait, then the limit of his capacity is touched and passed... He is expected to lend us his eyes and yet at the same time to present himself for us to behold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the narrative's main aim is to render the narrator's inner life, growth, or moral history (as Meredith's Harry Richmond), relying solely on first-person reportage can fail: the narrator can report but cannot fully dramatize his own consciousness. In such cases prefer methods that allow dramatization of the narrator's inner change or use other techniques to give the narrator sufficient substance and visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize central/internal affairs — show rather than only tell
rubrics_metrics.description: Drama we want, always drama, for the central, essential, paramount affair... Harry’s consciousness ought to be dramatized. Something is lost if it is represented solely by his account of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the core events that define character change or essential moral/emotional business, enact scenes that let readers judge and witness rather than depend solely on a narrator's retrospective account. Even a brilliant first-person account may not substitute for direct dramatization of inner processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine methods skillfully to correct weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Method can be imposed upon method, one kind upon another; in analyzing certain novelists one discovers how ingeniously they will correct the weakness of one method by the force of another and retain the advantages of both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use narration and scene in combination: dramatize parts of a pictorial method when intensity is needed; use pictorial summary to cover breadth while inserting scenes for emphasis. Study authors (Thackeray, Meredith, Dickens) to see how they mix devices to balance scope and intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat scenes with care; avoid repeating and wasting them
rubrics_metrics.description: On the whole, the possibilities of the scene are greatly abused in fiction... They are doubly abused; for the treatment of the scene is neglected, and yet it recurs again and again, much too often, and its value is wasted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let scenes become routine or negligently handled. Each enacted scene should be given proper treatment and reserved for moments that merit enactment; avoid repetitive, careless scenes that dilute dramatic power.
